units.title: The Communication Process and Its Barriers
topics: Eight reasons why communication skills matter to a computing professional

sections.title: Eight reasons why communication skills matter to a computing professional

summary: Communication succeeds only when the intended meaning is understood; feedback confirms it.
Messages travel in verbal, non-verbal and visual forms and along formal and informal channels.
Barriers can be removed by plain language, good channel choice, listening and cultural awareness.
The 7 Cs and a readability check are a practical test for any message before you send it.

units.title: Listening, Speaking and Presentation Skills
topics: Eight habits of a good presenter and listener

sections.title: Eight habits of a good presenter and listener

summary: Listening is an active skill built on attention, paraphrasing and questions.
Clear speaking comes from structure, pace, voice, body language and rehearsal.
A presentation starts from the audience and one key message; slides support rather than replace the speaker.
Group discussions and interviews reward preparation, honest and specific answers, and respect for others.

units.title: Professional Writing: Emails, Letters, CVs and Reports
topics: Eight rules of good professional writing

sections.title: Eight rules of good professional writing

summary: Good writing is organised into one-idea paragraphs, active sentences and lists where steps are listed.
Emails state the purpose and the required action in the first lines; letters and CVs follow standard layouts tailored to the reader.
Notices, agendas and minutes record who decides and who acts.
Reports lead with a summary; every borrowed idea or line of code needs a citation.

units.title: Workplace Communication, Teamwork and Etiquette
topics: Eight characteristics of an effective team

sections.title: Eight characteristics of an effective team

summary: Teams pass through predictable stages; clear goals, owners, rituals and early reporting make them productive.
Conflicts are managed by listening, focusing on interests and agreeing on written actions.
Feedback is most useful when specific, timely and about behaviour, not personality.
Time management is the art of choosing what matters and protecting time for it.
Courtesy, confidentiality and punctuality define professional reputation, in office and online.

units.title: Professional Ethics, Intellectual Property and Cyber Law
topics: Privacy, security and responsible data use
Eight responsibilities of an IT professional

sections.title: Privacy, security and responsible data use
Eight responsibilities of an IT professional

summary: Ethics asks what we ought to do; law sets the minimum, and professionals are expected to exceed it.
A structured method and a code such as ACM's turn vague unease into a defensible decision.
Copyright, patents, trademarks, trade secrets and licences define what you may do with others' work; plagiarism and piracy violate them.
Responsible practice means protecting privacy, securing data, testing for bias and speaking up about danger.
Real failures (Therac-25, VW, 737 MAX, Equifax) show what happens when these duties are ignored.
